title: Loop Engineering from First Principles — Kyle Mistele, HumanLayer

summary:
Kyle Mistele, co-founder and CTO of HumanLayer, presents "Loop Engineering from First Principles" at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. His core thesis is that current agent loops — exemplified by "blind Ralph loops" (bash loops feeding prompts to coding agents, popularized by Geoffrey Huntley) — produce massive, unreadable PRs unsuitable for teams with real production constraints like SLAs, regulatory obligations, and customers. He advocates applying control theory to agent loop design: a sensor measures current codebase state, a set point defines the desired state, the measured error drives a controller that emits a control signal, and an actuator applies an incremental change before the system remeasures. This pattern is already familiar in thermostats, Kubernetes auto-scaling, infrastructure-as-code, Postgres autovacuum, and React's virtual DOM — all of which change systems incrementally to avoid destabilization.

The practical demonstration covers HumanLayer's incremental migration of their RPC API to the Effect TypeScript framework. ast-grep (a Rust-based, tree-sitter-powered structural code search tool) serves as a language-agnostic sensor finding unmigrated procedures, with violations filtered, deterministically sorted, and tracked in version control. Before migration begins, a "disturbance dampener" gates new PRs to prevent regression by blocking PRs that introduce unmigrated procedures. The controller can pick the smallest unmigrated procedure to minimize risk, or use telemetry (error rates, instrumentation coverage) to prioritize procedures that would benefit most from improvement rather than one-to-one migration. The actuator is an agent plus a skill built from hand-written "golden patterns" — idiomatic before/after examples the agent replicates rather than generating idioms from scratch. The skill includes a structured response template; the loop deterministically commits, pushes, and creates a PR using the agent's final message as the PR description.

The loop runs as a GitHub Actions workflow scheduled daily, producing one small, reviewable PR each morning. Initial setup was high friction due to constant skill iteration. The solution is a feedback file tracked in version control and loaded into the actuator's context each run. Reviewers leave a /iterate comment on a PR, which triggers the workflow to reload all PR context and instruct the agent to fix code and update the feedback file. For flow control, the workflow checks whether any PR with the loop's label is still open before running; if so, it shuts down, ensuring at most one open PR per loop and preventing stacked, conflicting work. Velocity can scale by migrating multiple procedures per iteration with separate context windows, or running parallel workflows for different team members. Kyle notes that 150 RPC procedures migrated one per day would take approximately 6 months, motivating velocity scaling strategies. He references Peter Steinberger's call to design loops rather than prompt agents directly, Boris Turney's statement that his job is writing loops to prompt Claude, and Matt Pocock's argument that bad code is more expensive in the age of agents than ever before. The talk was verified against first-party sources: HumanLayer's official homepage and GitHub, the ast-grep and Effect-TS repositories, Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph blog post, and the AI Engineer conference website.
whyItMatters: The software engineering and AI concepts in this talk form a coherent system: control theory provides the theoretical framework (sensor-controller-actuator-feedback), which is instantiated through specific software engineering practices (ast-grep sensors, PR gating/disturbance dampeners, golden pattern skills, version-controlled feedback files, CI-scheduled execution, flow control for PR stacking). The AI concepts (agent-as-actuator, human-on-the-loop, context engineering, velocity scaling) describe how LLM-based agents fit into this framework as constrained, steerable components rather than autonomous decision-makers. Together, they address the fundamental tension between agent autonomy and production safety: the control loop provides the structure that makes agents safe enough for real codebases, while the feedback and flow control mechanisms make human oversight practical at scale. Without the control-theoretic framing, the individual practices (ast-grep, GitHub Actions, feedback files) are just tooling tips; without the concrete software engineering practices, the control theory is abstract. The talk's contribution is showing how they interlock to produce a production-grade agent loop pattern.
temporalContext: This talk was published on 2026-07-25 and recorded at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 (San Francisco, June 29–July 2, 2026). It is part of a mid-2026 wave of discourse on agent loop design, following Geoffrey Huntley's Ralph technique (July 2025), HumanLayer's Advanced Context Engineering blog post (August 2025), and the broader industry trend of moving from prompt-driven agent interactions to structured, control-theoretic loop architectures. At this time, Effect-TS was in v4 release candidate stage with agent-oriented migration tooling, ast-grep had 15.6k GitHub stars, and HumanLayer had recently raised profile through their 12-factor-agents framework (25.4k stars) and YC backing. The talk reflects the industry's shift from individual-agent productivity tools toward production-grade, team-safe agent infrastructure — a transition point where control theory and systems engineering principles are being applied to LLM-based agent loops for the first time at scale.

concepts.name: Control theory applied to agent loops
concepts.explanation: Translating classical control theory concepts (sensor, set point, measured error, controller, actuator, feedback loop) from engineering domains (thermostats, Kubernetes auto-scaling, Postgres autovacuum, React virtual DOM) to AI agent loop design. The codebase is the dynamic system; the agent is the actuator; the sensor measures codebase state.
concepts.importance: This is the foundational AI concept of the talk. It provides a rigorous, well-understood framework for designing agent loops that are stable, incremental, and steerable — moving beyond ad-hoc prompt piping.

concepts.name: Human-on-the-loop (human steering of autonomous agent loops)
concepts.explanation: Rather than full autonomy or full manual control, the pattern places humans 'on the loop' — the loop runs autonomously in CI but humans can intervene via /iterate comments and feedback files to re-steer the agent without taking over manual execution.
concepts.importance: Defines the human-AI collaboration model for production agent loops. It balances autonomy with oversight, making agent loops safe enough for production use.

concepts.name: Agent skills with golden patterns
concepts.explanation: Building agent 'skills' from hand-written idiomatic code examples (golden patterns) that the agent replicates, rather than relying on the agent's training data or documentation. The skill includes a structured response template that constrains the agent's output format.
concepts.importance: Represents a key approach to controlling agent output quality in production. By treating agents as pattern replicators, teams can achieve consistent, idiomatic results without fine-tuning.

concepts.name: Agent-as-actuator in control systems
concepts.explanation: In the control-theoretic framework, the AI agent serves as the actuator — the component that applies incremental changes to the system. The agent is not the entire loop; it is one component guided by deterministic sensors, controllers, and flow control mechanisms.
concepts.importance: Reframes the role of LLM-based agents from autonomous decision-makers to constrained actuators within a larger control system, which is a significant architectural shift for production agent design.

concepts.name: Context engineering for agent loops
concepts.explanation: The talk builds on HumanLayer's broader context engineering framework (Research/Plan/Implement workflow, frequent intentional compaction) by adding control-theoretic structure. The feedback file mechanism and telemetry-driven context are context engineering patterns applied within the control loop.
concepts.importance: Connects the talk's control-theoretic approach to the broader context engineering movement that HumanLayer has championed, providing additional conceptual grounding.

concepts.name: Velocity scaling for agent loops
concepts.explanation: Scaling agent loop throughput by migrating multiple procedures per iteration with separate context windows, or running parallel workflows for different team members. This trades off PR reviewability against velocity.
concepts.importance: Addresses the practical concern that one-PR-per-day is too slow for large migrations (150 procedures = 6 months). Scaling strategies make control-theoretic loops viable for enterprise-scale codebases.

concepts.name: Control-theoretic agent loop
concepts.explanation: Applying classical control theory (sensor, set point, measured error, controller, actuator, feedback) to agent loop design instead of ad-hoc prompt piping. The sensor measures codebase state, the controller computes incremental change, the actuator applies it, and the system remeasures — producing small, verifiable diffs rather than one giant PR.
concepts.importance: This is the central architectural thesis of the talk. It reframes agent loop design from prompt engineering to systems engineering, making loops suitable for production teams with SLAs and regulatory constraints.

concepts.name: Incremental migration via control loops
concepts.explanation: Migrating a codebase incrementally (one procedure at a time) using a control loop rather than a single large diff. Each iteration senses remaining violations, selects the smallest or highest-value target, applies the change, and creates a reviewable PR.
concepts.importance: Directly addresses the 40,000-line PR problem by making each change small, reviewable, and reversible. This is the practical pattern teams can adopt for any codebase-wide transformation.

concepts.name: Disturbance dampener (PR gating)
concepts.explanation: A CI gate that blocks new PRs from introducing code that violates the migration target (e.g., unmigrated RPC procedures), preventing regression before migration begins. Analogous to a control system's disturbance rejection.
concepts.importance: Prevents the codebase from regressing while migration is underway, ensuring the set point is monotonically approached rather than oscillating.

concepts.name: Golden patterns for actuator skills
concepts.explanation: Hand-written, idiomatic before/after code examples that guide the actuator agent's output. Rather than relying on documentation or the agent's training data, teams build golden patterns by hand to ensure the agent replicates the desired idiom precisely.
concepts.importance: Treats agents as pattern replicators rather than idiom generators. This is a key engineering practice for achieving consistent, high-quality agent output in production loops.

concepts.name: Version-controlled feedback file for human steering
concepts.explanation: A markdown file tracked in version control that is deterministically loaded into the actuator agent's context each run. Reviewers leave /iterate comments on PRs, triggering the workflow to reload PR context and instruct the agent to fix code and update the feedback file, keeping human corrections low-friction and auditable.
concepts.importance: Solves the high-friction problem of re-steering agent loops. Makes human feedback persistent, version-controlled, and automatically incorporated into future iterations.

concepts.name: Flow control for PR stacking prevention
concepts.explanation: Before running, the workflow checks whether any PR with the loop's label is still open; if so, it shuts down. This ensures at most one open PR per loop at a time, preventing stacked, conflicting PRs when humans are unavailable to review.
concepts.importance: Prevents duplicate work, merge conflicts, and PR pile-up — a critical operational concern for teams running agent loops in CI.

concepts.name: CI-scheduled agent loop execution
concepts.explanation: Running the control loop as a GitHub Actions workflow on a daily schedule, producing one small incremental PR each morning. The loop performs sense, control, actuate in a single CI run.
concepts.importance: Makes agent loops a first-class CI concern rather than a manual or interactive process. Enables consistent, automated, incremental progress on codebase transformations.

concepts.name: Telemetry-driven controller prioritization
concepts.explanation: The controller can use telemetry data (error rates, instrumentation coverage) to prioritize which procedures to migrate first, passing that context to the actuator so it improves code beyond a one-to-one migration.
concepts.importance: Elevates the controller from a simple FIFO queue to an optimization system that targets highest-value changes, improving code quality rather than just performing mechanical migration.

concepts.name: Blind Ralph loop critique
concepts.explanation: Kyle critiques 'blind Ralph loops' — bash loops that feed prompts to coding agents (popularized by Geoffrey Huntley) — as suitable for individuals but unsuitable for teams with production constraints because they produce massive, non-incremental diffs and lack flow control, feedback mechanisms, and regression prevention.
concepts.importance: Establishes the problem statement and motivates the control-theoretic alternative. The critique is nuanced — Ralph is acknowledged as innovative but insufficient for production teams.

concepts.name: ast-grep as deterministic structural sensor
concepts.explanation: Using ast-grep (a Rust-based, tree-sitter-powered CLI tool for structural code search) as a language-agnostic sensor that detects unmigrated code patterns. Violations are filtered, deterministically sorted, and tracked in version control for the controller to consume.
concepts.importance: Demonstrates how to build a deterministic, reproducible sensor for agent loops — a prerequisite for control-theoretic agent design. ast-grep's tree-sitter basis makes it language-agnostic.

sections.title: Introduction: The 40,000 line PR problem
sections.summary: Kyle introduces himself as co-founder of HumanLayer and frames the problem: agent loops produce massive PRs nobody can review. Ralph works for individuals but not teams with real customers, regulatory obligations, and SLAs. He calls for building loops for the real world.

sections.title: Loop discourse, hype, and expense
sections.summary: Kyle references viral loop posts, Peter Steinberger's call to design loops rather than prompt agents, Boris Turney's statement that his job is writing loops to prompt Claude, and notes that all this generated code is expensive and often unread. Matt Pocock's point that bad code is more expensive in the age of agents is cited.

sections.title: Control theory fundamentals and examples
sections.summary: Kyle introduces control theory: a sensor measures current state, a set point defines desired state, the difference is measured error, a controller emits a control signal, an actuator applies incremental change, then the system remeasures. Examples include thermostats, Kubernetes auto-scaling, IaC, Postgres autovacuum, and React's virtual DOM. Control loops contrast with 'blind Ralph loops' by changing systems incrementally.

sections.title: Building agentic control loops
sections.summary: Kyle explains how to build agentic control loops: define a set point for desired codebase property, add a sensor (deterministic like ESLint/AST grep, or non-deterministic using agents), and design a well-tuned controller. Components can blur together, as with Aiden by React Doctor functioning as both sensor and controller. Use cases include API compliance, MCP spec compliance, language mirroring, and fork maintenance.

sections.title: Practical example: migrating to Effect with AST grep
sections.summary: Kyle demonstrates HumanLayer's incremental migration from RPC API to Effect. AST grep serves as a language-agnostic sensor finding unmigrated procedures. Violations are filtered and sorted deterministically, tracked in version control. Before migrating, a 'disturbance dampener' gates new PRs to prevent adding unmigrated procedures. Controller options include picking the first violation, or using AST grep to find the smallest unmigrated procedure to reduce risk.

sections.title: Controller telemetry, actuator design, and golden patterns
sections.summary: The controller can use telemetry to prioritize procedures with the most errors or least instrumentation, passing that context to the actuator so it improves code beyond a one-to-one migration. The actuator is an agent plus a skill; HumanLayer builds golden patterns by hand—idiomatic examples the agent replicates. The skill includes a response template, and the loop deterministically commits, pushes, and creates a PR using the agent's final message as the PR description.

sections.title: Wiring the loop into CI with human feedback
sections.summary: Kyle recommends running the loop in GitHub Actions or equivalent CI, scheduled daily, producing one small incremental PR each morning. Initial setup was high friction due to constant skill updates. The fix is a feedback file tracked in version control, loaded into the actuator's context each run. Reviewers leave /iterate comments on PRs, which triggers the workflow to reload PR context and instruct the agent to fix code and update the feedback file, keeping steering low-friction and auditable.

sections.title: Flow control, scaling velocity, and conclusion
sections.summary: Kyle addresses stacked PRs: the workflow checks for open PRs with its label before running, shutting down if one exists, ensuring at most one open PR per loop. Velocity scales by migrating multiple procedures per iteration, using separate context windows, or running workflows in parallel for different team members. He wraps up by summarizing the control loop approach—incremental, readable, adaptive, re-steerable—and mentions HumanLayer is hiring in San Francisco.

organization.name: HumanLayer
organization.summary: HumanLayer is a Y Combinator (F24 batch)-backed company founded in 2023 and headquartered in San Francisco, California. It builds an AI IDE, collaboration platform, and building blocks for software factories, enabling engineering teams to ship 2-3x faster with coding agents while maintaining code quality and architecture standards. The company is co-founded by Dexter Horthy (CEO) and Kyle Mistele (CTO), the speaker in this video. HumanLayer maintains high-profile open-source projects including 12-factor-agents (25.4k stars), the humanlayer coding agent platform (11.3k stars), advanced-context-engineering-for-coding-agents (2.5k stars), agentcontrolplane (461 stars), skills (410 stars), and fold (48 stars), the latter being an Effect-native agent core confirming their codebase is built on Effect-TS. The company coined the term 'Context Engineering' in April 2025 and has nearly 1M cumulative YouTube views and over 25k GitHub stars across their open-source work.

technologies.label: Control-Theory Agent Loop Architecture
technologies.primary: Control-theoretic agent loop (sensor, set point, measured error, controller, actuator, feedback)
technologies.summary: The primary technology family is the control-theoretic agent loop architecture that Kyle Mistele advocates as a replacement for blind Ralph loops. It applies classical control theory (sensor, set point, measured error, controller, actuator, feedback) to AI agent loop design: a deterministic sensor measures codebase state, a controller computes the error against a set point and selects the smallest or highest-value change, an actuator (agent + skill) applies the incremental change, and the system remeasures. Supporting techniques include disturbance dampeners (PR gating to prevent regression), version-controlled feedback files for human steering, flow control to prevent PR stacking, telemetry-driven prioritization, CI-scheduled execution via GitHub Actions, and golden patterns for actuator skills. The pattern produces small, reviewable, incremental PRs suitable for production teams with SLAs and regulatory constraints, directly addressing the 40,000-line PR problem.
technologies.role: This is the central architectural thesis of the talk. Kyle Mistele presents control-theoretic agent loops as the fundamental pattern for building production-grade agent loops, using HumanLayer's RPC-to-Effect migration as the practical demonstration.

technologies.label: ast-grep Structural Code Search
technologies.summary: ast-grep is a Rust-based, tree-sitter-powered CLI tool for structural code search, lint, and rewriting that serves as the deterministic sensor in the talk's control loop architecture. It finds unmigrated RPC procedures by matching AST patterns, with violations filtered and deterministically sorted and tracked in version control. Kyle describes it as language-agnostic and a great tool for building loops. Verified externally as a real tool with 15.6k GitHub stars, supporting 20+ languages including TypeScript, with a Node.js API for programmatic AST traversal.
technologies.role: ast-grep is the concrete sensor tool used in the practical demonstration of the control loop. Kyle demonstrates how it finds unmigrated procedures deterministically and how its output feeds the controller.

technologies.label: Effect-TS Framework
technologies.summary: Effect-TS is a production-grade TypeScript framework (15.4k GitHub stars) that is the migration target in the talk's practical demonstration. HumanLayer is migrating their RPC API to Effect, and their codebase is Effect-native (confirmed by humanlayer/fold repo). The Effect ecosystem provides an agent-oriented migration guide with 290 import mappings and 53 API renames, confirming that agent-driven migration is a real practice. Effect provides typed errors, dependency injection, structured concurrency, scheduling, tracing, and schema validation.
technologies.role: Effect-TS is the target framework for the incremental migration that demonstrates the control loop in practice. The migration from HumanLayer's RPC API to Effect is the central practical example in the talk.

technologies.label: HumanLayer Agent Platform
technologies.summary: HumanLayer is an AI coding agent platform (YC-backed, co-founded by Dexter Horthy as CEO and Kyle Mistele as CTO) that builds production-grade agent infrastructure. Their GitHub organization has 21 public repos including humanlayer/humanlayer (11.3k stars), humanlayer/12-factor-agents (25.4k stars), humanlayer/fold (Effect-native agent core), and humanlayer/skills (410 stars). The talk's practical demonstration is HumanLayer's internal RPC-to-Effect migration loop, and their skills repo directly implements the golden pattern actuator approach. The 12-factor-agents framework and Advanced Context Engineering methodology provide the conceptual foundation that the control-theoretic loop approach builds upon.
technologies.role: HumanLayer is the featured organization. Kyle Mistele is CTO and co-founder. The talk's practical demonstration is HumanLayer's internal migration loop, and their open-source repos provide evidence that the patterns described are real production practices.
